analysis.one_liner: Exempts farm and livestock truckers from federal driving-hour limits year-round within 150 miles.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to let agricultural and livestock haulers bypass federal driving-hour rules year-round died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules limit how many hours a truck driver can work before resting, to prevent fatigue-related crashes. Current law already waives those limits for farm and livestock hauling during planting and harvest seasons within 150 miles of the source or destination. This bill would make that waiver available all year and would widen the definition of "agricultural commodity" to cover fish, insects, milk, eggs, honey, forestry products, and animal feed. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, ranchers, livestock haulers, and agricultural processors gain: they could move crops, livestock, feed, and other farm goods on their own schedules year-round without the federal limits on driving and on-duty hours, cutting transport costs and delays for perishable loads.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the 150 air-mile hours-of-service exemption for agricultural commodities and farm supplies available year-round, instead of only during planting and harvest periods set by each state.
Measures the 150-mile radius from the source or the destination of the goods, making the exemption easier to use on more trips.

Directs the Department of Transportation to expand the definition of "agricultural commodity" to include fish, insects, livestock, milk, eggs, honey, forestry, aquaculture, horticulture, and floriculture products, minimally processed fruits and vegetables, and animal feed — extending the exemption to far more hauling.

analysis.who_pays: Other people on rural roads and the drivers themselves bear the added risk of fatigue-related crashes, since hours-of-service limits are the federal safeguard designed to keep tired truckers off the road. Any crash costs land on the general public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rural road users and the drivers

drawbacks.text: The exemption removes the federal limits on driving and on-duty time that exist to prevent fatigue-related truck crashes; extending it year-round means those safeguards are off for a much larger share of agricultural hauling.
The bill was introduced but received no committee hearing or vote, so no committee record exists weighing the safety concerns against the industry's scheduling needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real case for the bill: perishable and live cargo cannot wait for a clock, and a rigid hours limit on a short 150-mile farm haul can strand livestock or spoil crops. But the bill answers a scheduling problem by simply switching off the federal fatigue-safety rule for an entire industry year-round, and it never went through a committee where that tradeoff could be examined. The safety cost is real but the stakes are narrower than a universal rule change, since the exemption covers only trips within 150 air miles of the farm or destination.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took the bill up, so it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2021 by Senator Fischer with Senator Tester and two other senators as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Twenty-five senators cosponsored the bill, 22 Republicans and 3 Democrats.
No further action was taken: the committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal hours-of-service protections stay in place year-round for agricultural hauling, so road users keep the existing fatigue-safety safeguards. Agricultural haulers are the losers here: they did not get the year-round exemption they sought, and similar relief has been pursued in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing truck safety rules stayed intact

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the agricultural hours-of-service exemption year-round.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred: no hearing, no markup, no vote to send it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan at the top — Senator Fischer (R-NE) and Senator Tester (D-MT) led it — but the cosponsor list skewed heavily Republican, 22 Republicans to 3 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would lift federal driving-hour limits from farm and livestock haulers year-round within 150 miles, letting them run longer and more flexible schedules. The cost of that flexibility — fatigue-crash risk — falls on the drivers and other road users, not the industry.

industries.industry: Farmers, ranchers, and specialty producers (livestock, aquaculture, forestry, horticulture)
industries.note: Broader commodity definitions and a year-round exemption would cut transport delays and costs for perishable and live cargo, and cheaper transport can slightly lower food prices. Ordinary people benefit only indirectly here.
Year-round exemption would give processors a more reliable, less regulated supply of raw commodities moving to their facilities.
